sentences.text: Chendytes was a goose-sized flightless marine duck that once lived along the California coast, the Channel Islands, and possibly southern Oregon. While the species Chendytes lawi was the largest, the related Chendytes milleri was smaller and retained wings that had not degenerated as much.

Humans exploited Chendytes lawi for at least 8,000 years, a duration unmatched by any other megafaunal genus in the North American archaeological record. Fossil evidence of hundreds of bones and eggshells on San Miguel Island indicates the existence of nesting colonies, with one dated to approximately 12,000 radiocarbon years ago.
Chendytes lawi specialized in eating sessile invertebrates and likely had a remarkable ability to wrench them off hard substrates.

Chendytes lawi was formerly classified within the subfamily Merginae. However, analysis of ancient DNA suggests Chendytes is a basal member of the tribe Anatini, representing a case of convergent evolution in feeding behavior rather than belonging to the tribe Mergini.

The genus Chendytes existed from the Gelasian to the Holocene, spanning from 2.58 to 0 million years ago. Chendytes lived during the Pleistocene and survived into the Holocene, going extinct around 450–250 BCE.
